item.title: The kernel: what runs, and what is kept
item.description:
Each run takes the notebook’s current code cells and does the least work that brings every result up to date. Four steps get there: the analysis of the cells, the generated program, the cell keys, and the value store.

The dependency graph

Package analysis finds each cell’s definitions and free identifiers from the parse alone. It needs no type information, so it works on code that does not compile yet.

A cell depends on the cells that define the names it reads. That gives the graph, the order of execution, and the static errors: cycles, double definitions and assignments to another cell’s variable (see Cells). The order is therefore a function of the code, never of the order cells were run in or appear in.

The generated program

Package gen writes the Go program the kernel compiles:

  • each cell becomes a function;
  • its variables become package-level variables, so every cell can read them and their values outlive the call. That needs their types, so gen type-checks the cells one by one, in dependency order, with go/types;
  • the cells’ text is kept as it is and edited in place: := becomes = , var x T becomes x = *new(T) (so running the cell again resets it), constants move to package level, and the display value is wrapped in a call that shows it;
  • //line nb.md:L:C directives point every line back into the notebook.

The kernel compiles this program into a worker process and drives it through package runtime: one JSON request per line on the worker’s standard input (run, get, set, exit) and one reply per line on its standard output. What a cell prints goes to a pipe of its own, so it can never be mistaken for a reply.

Go’s build cache makes rebuilding after a one-cell edit cost about a tenth of a second.

A cell’s key

A cell’s key is a hash of:

  • its source;
  • the import paths of the packages it refers to;
  • the Go toolchain’s version;
  • the work module’s go.sum, when the cell uses a package outside the standard library (any module could be behind such a package, transitively, so the whole go.sum is the honest summary);
  • the keys of the cells it reads.

Its position is not part of the key, so moving cells runs nothing; neither does an import another cell adds. Upgrading Go, or a dependency, runs again what it could change, and only that: a cell using only the standard library is not run again by a go.sum change. Because a key includes the keys of its inputs, a change propagates to exactly the cells downstream of it.

What runs

A cell whose key… …
did not change keeps its result and is not run
changed runs, and so does every cell whose key changes because of it
did not change, but made a volatile value that a running cell reads runs again, to make that value (see below)
reads a cell that failed is not run, and reports not run: cell N failed

When the program changes, the worker is rebuilt and restarted. The variables made by unchanged cells are handed to the new worker instead of being computed again.

A worker that dies (os.Exit, a crash outside the recovered call) is restarted on the next run.

Kept values

To hand a value over, or to keep it on disk, the kernel encodes it:

  • with its own MarshalBinary when it has one;
  • with gob when every field it can hold is exported (gob would silently drop the others).

Anything else — a func, a channel, unexported state — is volatile: its cell runs again, but only when a cell that reads it has to run.

On disk

Results and values are kept in the work directory, so a new kernel, or the next notebook run, starts where the last one stopped. The notebook command gives each notebook its own work directory under the user’s cache directory.

The assumption

All of this assumes a cell computes the same values from the same inputs. A cell that reads the clock or an unseeded random generator does not; such a cell should be run explicitly — Kernel.RunCell runs a cell again even if nothing changed, together with every cell that reads it.

Using the kernel from Go 

k, err := kernel.New(kernel.Options{Dir: work, Name: "analysis.md"})
if err != nil { … }
defer k.Close()

rep, err := k.Run(cells) // cells: []gen.Code{{Source: …, Line: …}, …}
for _, r := range rep.Results {
 // r.Ran, r.Took, r.Output, r.Display, r.Error
}

Report.Built says whether the worker was rebuilt, Report.Build how long generating and building took, and Report.Diags holds the static errors.
